chunks.text: 2 Methodology 2.1 Overview As shown in Fig. 2 , visual and textual features guide progressive decoding. RDABs regulate cross-modal fusion, while TSRAs operate on separate skip pathways, refining encoder features before their integration into decoder blocks. Finally, subpixel upsampling restores the spatial resolution, and the segmentation head generates the final pixel-wise predictions. 2.2 Reliability-guided Fusion Gate (RFG) Given medical images 𝐈 ∈ ℝ B × C I × H × W \mathbf{I}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times C_{I}\times H\times W} and tokenized descriptions 𝐓 \mathbf{T} , ConvNeXt-Tiny [ 8 ] extracts visual features 𝐈 s ′ \mathbf{I}^{\prime}_{s} across four encoder stages, s ∈ { 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 } s\in\{1,2,3,4\} , while BioViL CXR-BERT [ 1 ] generates text embeddings 𝐓 ′ ∈ ℝ B × L × D T \mathbf{T}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L\times D_{T}} . Here, B B denotes batch size, C I C_{I} the image channels, H , W H,W the spatial dimensions, and L , D T L,D_{T} the text length and embedding dimension. Decoding starts from the deepest visual features 𝐈 4 ′ \mathbf{I}^{\prime}_{4} , reshaped into 𝐕 ∈ ℝ B × N 4 × C 4 \mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times N_{4}\times C_{4}} , where N 4 = H 4 ​ W 4 N_{4}\penalty\ =\penalty\ H_{4}W_{4} is the number of visual tokens. Meanwhile, text embeddings pass through a learnable linear layer, LeakyReLU, SSMixer, and GELU to produce 𝐓 p ∈ ℝ B × L p × C 4 \mathbf{T}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L_{p}\times C_{4}} , where L p L_{p} is the resulting sequence length. SSMixer models dependencies among textual tokens to provide context-aware representations at the current visual scale. Within RDAB, normalized and position-encoded visual tokens undergo multi-head self-attention. The output is normalized and added to 𝐕 \mathbf{V} through a residual connection, yielding contextual features 𝐕 c \mathbf{V}_{c} .

Cross-attention then uses normalized, position-encoded 𝐕 c \mathbf{V}_{c} as queries, position-encoded 𝐓 p \mathbf{T}_{p} as keys, and 𝐓 p \mathbf{T}_{p} as values to generate text-conditioned features 𝐂 \mathbf{C} . To assess their consistency with visual information, RFG combines both representations and their feature-level relationships: 𝐀 = Concat ⁡ ( 𝐕 c , 𝐂 , | 𝐕 c − 𝐂 | , 𝐕 c ⊙ 𝐂 ) . \mathbf{A}=\operatorname{Concat}\left(\mathbf{V}_{c},\mathbf{C},|\mathbf{V}_{c}-\mathbf{C}|,\mathbf{V}_{c}\odot\mathbf{C}\right). (1) A lightweight reliability head then estimates a response for each visual token: 𝐑 = σ ⁡ ( Linear ⁡ ( GELU ⁡ ( Linear ⁡ ( LN ⁡ ( 𝐀 ) ) ) ) ) . \mathbf{R}=\sigma\left(\operatorname{Linear}\left(\operatorname{GELU}\left(\operatorname{Linear}(\operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{A}))\right)\right)\right). (2) The complementary uncertainty representation is defined as 𝐔 = 1 − 𝐑 \mathbf{U}=1-\mathbf{R} , with higher values indicating lower estimated reliability. The reliability response subsequently regulates cross-modal fusion through 𝐆 = 0.5 + 𝐑 , 𝐘 = 𝐕 + α ⁡ ( 𝐆 ⊙ 𝐂 ) , \mathbf{G}=0.5+\mathbf{R},\qquad\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{V}+\alpha(\mathbf{G}\odot\mathbf{C}), (3) where ⊙ \odot denotes element-wise multiplication, σ \sigma the sigmoid function, and α \alpha a learnable scalar. The bounded gate 𝐆 ∈ [ 0.5 , 1.5 ] \mathbf{G}\in[0.5,1.5] regulates cross-modal contributions without entirely suppressing or excessively amplifying them. 2.3 Text-guided Skip Refinement Adapter (TSRA) While RFG regulates cross-modal fusion, TSRA refines high-resolution skip features 𝐈 s ′ \mathbf{I}^{\prime}_{s} for s ∈ { 1 , 2 , 3 } s\in\{1,2,3\} to preserve relevant spatial details. The shared text embedding 𝐓 ′ \mathbf{T}^{\prime} is averaged across L L tokens to obtain 𝐭 g \mathbf{t}_{g} , which is normalized and projected into a stage-specific channel response.

A sigmoid activation and a 0.5 0.5 shift are then applied, followed by reshaping to enable channel-wise modulation of the spatial skip features, yielding 𝐠 ¯ s ∈ [ 0.5 , 1.5 ] B × C s × 1 × 1 \overline{\mathbf{g}}_{s}\in[0.5,1.5]^{B\times C_{s}\times 1\times 1} : 𝐠 ¯ s = Reshape ⁡ ( 0.5 + σ ⁡ ( Linear ⁡ ( LN ⁡ ( 𝐭 g ) ) ) ) . \overline{\mathbf{g}}_{s}=\operatorname{Reshape}\left(0.5+\sigma\left(\operatorname{Linear}(\operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{t}_{g}))\right)\right). (4) In parallel, a depthwise 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution extracts local spatial details from 𝐈 s ′ \mathbf{I}^{\prime}_{s} , followed by batch normalization and GELU. A pointwise 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution then combines information across channels, followed by another normalization to produce 𝐃 s \mathbf{D}_{s} . The text-conditioned gate 𝐠 ¯ s \overline{\mathbf{g}}_{s} modulates these features through a scaled residual connection: 𝐈 ~ s ′ = GELU ⁡ ( 𝐈 s ′ + β ⁡ ( 𝐠 ¯ s ⊙ 𝐃 s ) ) ∈ ℝ B × C s × H s × W s . \widetilde{\mathbf{I}}^{\prime}_{s}=\operatorname{GELU}\left(\mathbf{I}^{\prime}_{s}+\beta\left(\overline{\mathbf{g}}_{s}\odot\mathbf{D}_{s}\right)\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times C_{s}\times H_{s}\times W_{s}}. (5) Here, β \beta is a learnable residual scale, and ⊙ \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. Zero-initialized gate projections and small initial residual scales allow gradual refinement. Finally, the refined skip features 𝐈 ~ s ′ \widetilde{\mathbf{I}}^{\prime}_{s} are fused with the upsampled decoder features without additional supervision. 2.4 Decoder Block The decoder progressively restores spatial details through three stages, s ∈ { 4 , 3 , 2 } s\in\{4,3,2\} . At each stage, RDAB uses the shared text embedding 𝐓 ′ \mathbf{T}^{\prime} to produce reliability-guided visual tokens 𝐘 s ∈ ℝ B × N s × C s \mathbf{Y}_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times N_{s}\times C_{s}} , where N s = H s ​ W s N_{s}=H_{s}W_{s} denotes the token count and C s C_{s} the channel dimension.

These tokens are reshaped into spatial features 𝐙 s ∈ ℝ B × C s × H s × W s \mathbf{Z}_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times C_{s}\times H_{s}\times W_{s}} and upsampled through transposed convolution. The resulting features are concatenated with the corresponding TSRA-refined skip features 𝐈 ~ s − 1 ′ \widetilde{\mathbf{I}}^{\prime}_{s-1} and convolved: 𝐃 s − 1 = ConvBlock ⁡ ( Concat ⁡ ( UpConv ⁡ ( 𝐙 s ) , 𝐈 ~ s − 1 ′ ) ) \mathbf{D}_{s-1}=\operatorname{ConvBlock}\left(\operatorname{Concat}\left(\operatorname{UpConv}(\mathbf{Z}_{s}),\widetilde{\mathbf{I}}^{\prime}_{s-1}\right)\right) (6) The fused features are converted back into visual tokens for the next RDAB, progressively incorporating finer spatial information. Finally, subpixel upsampling restores the input resolution, and a sigmoid-activated segmentation head generates pixel-wise foreground probabilities: 𝐌 ^ = σ ⁡ ( SegHead ⁡ ( SubPixelUp ⁡ ( 𝐃 1 ) ) ) . \widehat{\mathbf{M}}=\sigma\left(\operatorname{SegHead}\left(\operatorname{SubPixelUp}(\mathbf{D}_{1})\right)\right). (7) 2.5 Objective Function RELiF is trained using the Spectral-Entropic Uncertainty (SEU) objective [ 2 ] , which combines three complementary loss terms. Dice loss maximizes overlap between the predicted mask 𝐌 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{M}} and ground truth 𝐌 \mathbf{M} , while spectral loss encourages structural consistency by comparing their Fourier magnitude spectra. An entropy-inspired term further promotes confident foreground predictions. The overall objective is defined as ℒ total = ℒ Dice + λ F ​ ℒ Spectral + λ E ​ ℒ Entropy , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Dice}}+\lambda_{F}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Spectral}}+\lambda_{E}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Entropy}}, (8) where λ F \lambda_{F} and λ E \lambda_{E} control the contributions of the spectral and entropy terms, respectively. The entropy-inspired term is applied only to the final segmentation probabilities and is separate from the RFG-derived uncertainty representation.

RFG and TSRA are learned end-to-end without direct supervision. 3 Experiments and Results 3.1 Datasets Experiments were conducted on three public datasets: QaTa-COV19 [ 3 ] , MosMedData+ [ 9 ] , and Kvasir-SEG [ 6 ] , covering chest X-ray, CT, and endoscopic segmentation. Following the LViT protocol [ 7 ] , we adopt the same dataset splits and use text annotations from [ 7 ] for infection segmentation and [ 10 ] for polyp segmentation. The dataset splits are: QaTa-COV19: Training=5716; Validation=1429; Test=2113 MosMedData+: Training=2183; Validation=273; Test=273 Kvasir-SEG: Training=800; Validation=100; Test=100. 3.2 Implementation Details The framework was implemented in PyTorch, with each dataset trained independently on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. All input images and masks were resized to 224 × 224 224\times 224 pixels. Training was conducted for 200 epochs, using batch sizes of 32 for training and 8 for validation and testing. We used the AdamW optimizer with a cosine annealing learning-rate scheduler. Initial learning rates were 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} for QaTa-COV19 and Kvasir-SEG and 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} for MosMedData+. The SEU loss weights were set to λ F = 0.3 \lambda_{F}=0.3 and λ E = 0.1 \lambda_{E}=0.1 . RELiF achieves the highest Dice and mIoU scores on QaTa-COV19 and Kvasir-SEG, while maintaining competitive performance on MosMedData+ with only 18.1 G FLOPs. Qualitative comparisons in Fig. 3 further illustrate the segmentation results across all three datasets. To assess robustness under limited supervision, Table 2 compares RELiF with BiCLIP and LViT using 50% and 10% training data. RELiF achieves the best Dice and mIoU on two datasets at 50% and all three at 10%.

We further evaluated stability across five independent training runs, obtaining Dice standard deviations of 0.12, 0.14, and 0.24 percentage points on QaTa-COV19, MosMedData+, and Kvasir-SEG, respectively, indicating low run-to-run variability. The ablation study in Table 4 confirms the complementary contributions of RFG and TSRA, with their combination achieving the best performance. Furthermore, removing textual guidance or introducing mismatched text during training reduces segmentation accuracy, highlighting the importance of relevant textual information. Table 3 further evaluates the ability of RFG-derived uncertainty to distinguish erroneous pixels from correct predictions, reporting AUROC values of 0.7724–0.8473 and AUPRC scores 3.04–5.51 times their prevalence-based random baselines. These results suggest consistent error-discrimination ability across the three datasets. Finally, we conducted a pixel-level risk–coverage analysis on Kvasir-SEG by progressively excluding high-uncertainty pixels. At 90% coverage, retained-pixel error risk decreased by 45.2%, with selective Dice reaching 93.87%. Further reducing coverage to 70% increased risk reduction to 71.7%, although selective Dice declined, potentially due to the exclusion of correctly predicted foreground pixels. The results suggest benefits from complementary mechanisms under limited supervision. Sensitivity to mismatched text indicates that gains depend on relevant guidance rather than text alone. RFG-derived uncertainty helps identify unreliable regions, although excessive rejection may remove correctly segmented foreground. These findings motivate further reliability-aware segmentation research.
